comment: NIM CONTRACT fixture. Every construct the M12 symbol/relationship contract claims, in one compiler-validated file. The SOURCE is accepted by the real Nim 2.2.12 compiler (`nim check`, 0 errors — recorded at /home/ishaq2321/bb_tests/nim/fixture-src/contract.nim), so nothing pinned here is a construct the language rejects. Expectations are written from NIM SEMANTICS (what a declaration IS) and the kind-mapping table in docs/analyzers/nim.md, not copied from analyzer output: the point of a fixture is to fail when the analyzer drifts from the language.

expectSymbols.name: Color
expectSymbols.comment: a `type X = enum` is an enum

expectSymbols.name: Shape
expectSymbols.comment: `ref object` has identity + inheritance + dynamic dispatch -> class (a plain `object` would be struct)

expectSymbols.name: Pair
expectSymbols.comment: `tuple[x, y: int]` is a struct: it has named fields, it is destructurable (`let (a, b) = pair`) and its fields are readable as `pair.x`. The kind was WRONG until the mutation run: the classifier never saw through the grammar's `type_expression` wrapper, so it fell through to a bare `type` and the documented rule had no test behind it

expectSymbols.name: Addable
expectSymbols.comment: a `concept` is a compile-time structural interface

expectSymbols.name: describe
expectSymbols.comment: `method` -> method (dynamic dispatch on the first parameter's type)

expectSymbols.name: Anon
expectSymbols.comment: the ORDINARY unnamed tuple spelling, `(int, string)`, which the grammar types as tuple_construction rather than tuple_type. The compiler accepts this with 0 errors and rejects `tuple[int, string]` with 3, so it is the form real code uses — and before the mutation run it published a bare `type` while the named spelling beside it published a struct

expectSymbols.name: area
expectSymbols.docstringEndsWith: Exercised as a doc comment through the real CLI.
expectSymbols.comment: Nim's `##` doc comment reaches the symbol. Losing it is invisible in a symbol count, which is exactly why it needed a pin

expectSymbols.name: fileStem
expectSymbols.comment: the field genuinely EXISTS — it is `FileInfo.fileStem` at line 74. Asserting it is what makes the shadow pin meaningful: the `uses stemOf -> fileStem` forbid is only a real assertion because there is a real field for the misattribution to have landed on, and without this pin a fix that deleted the field outright would satisfy the forbid vacuously

expectSymbols.name: describe
expectSymbols.comment: `overrides` endpoints are receiver-qualified (`Rect.describe`) because the bare name `describe` cannot address either end, so a consumer walking INBOUND has no way to reach that endpoint unless some symbol publishes the qualified spelling. Measured with script/m14/incoming-check.ts on nim/lib/pure (105 files, 6,638 symbols) before this field existed: 14 of 14 `overrides` edges reported UNRESOLVED. The worker's `scope`-derived fallback cannot recover it, because a method's owner is `ownerName`, not `scope`.

forbidSymbols.name: s
forbidSymbols.comment: function-LOCAL `let s` is an execution artifact, never a symbol (LocalsAreNotSymbols)

forbidSymbols.name: x
forbidSymbols.comment: a macro/template parameter is not a symbol

forbidSymbols.name: e
forbidSymbols.comment: `except … as e` binds a local, not a symbol

forbidSymbols.name: retTrue
forbidSymbols.comment: a macro imported from another file is not declared in THIS file

forbidSymbols.name: Anon
forbidSymbols.comment: the negative twin of the pin above: Anon must be a struct, never a bare type. Two spellings of the same language construct, pinned in both directions, so a half-fix that handles only tuple_type or only tuple_construction fails here

forbidSymbols.name: T
forbidSymbols.comment: a generic PARAMETER is bound by `type Registry*[T]`, not declared by it, so there is nothing for a reference to resolve to
the blank identifier appears in every destructuring pattern and every `proc f(_: int)` signature; it declares nothing

expectRelationships.comment: owner -> field
owner -> enum member
`ref object of Shape` is a real inheritance edge
a method override is owner-qualified: `Receiver.method` (the name alone cannot address either end)
a parameter's declared type is a dependency; the tier is `reference_qualified` because the type name is qualified by a declaration rather than by an import
`Rect(...)` is object construction
a `var b: Builder` annotation is a declared-type dependency
a parameter's declared type is a dependency; the tier is `reference_qualified` because the type name is qualified by a declaration rather than by an import

`import std/[os, strutils]` is a module LIST: one edge per element, and the kind is the FIRST-CLASS `imports` (the LSP usages file-level section reads relationship_type IN ('imports','exports'), so a `references` edge here would be invisible to it). The TARGET is the MODULE NAME `os`, which is what the module symbol is published as; the written path is kept on `meta.nimModulePath`

a single-segment RELATIVE import is one edge whose target is the module NAME. This row USED to pin the verbatim spelling `./helpers`; that contract is withdrawn because the graph published no module symbol, so a verbatim path target had no candidate to bind to and 8,404 of 13,364 corpus `imports` edges were permanently unresolved (census.ts, 6,063 files). `meta.nimModulePath` keeps the written path
a parent-relative import is one edge, not dropped for having no `/` segment, and it targets the module NAME `shared` for the same reason as `./helpers` above
a plain call to a proc this file declares
an iterator is callable and is a `function` symbol
a UFCS call — `b.parts.join(",")` has no dot-call node, the member leaf is the callee
a bare read of a module-level `let` is a value dependency
the member leaf of a UFCS read (`b.parts.join`) is a `uses` edge, distinct from the `calls` edge to the same expression

the same declared-type reference class as `area -> Rect`, but a DIFFERENT evidence tier: `Rect` is resolved through the `./helpers`/`./mac` import graph, so the edge is marked import_based. Two tiers for one kind is the point of pinning evidenceClass at all

the line of the MODULE TOKEN, not of the `import` keyword. A multi-line import puts the paths on later lines than the keyword (the corpus's own compiler/nimsets.nim has `import` on 12 and its paths on 13), so anchoring to the directive points a reader at the wrong line. Target is the module NAME `globs`
a from-import's line is still the module token's, and a second line pin so the rule cannot be satisfied by anchoring every import to the file's first line. Target is the module NAME `mac`
a field's line is the field's own
an override's line is the DERIVED method's line, not the base's — 51 is Rect's describe, and pinning the base's line (50) would let a rule that reads the wrong node pass
a construction's line is the call's
a read's line is the identifier's
a parameter's type reference is anchored to the PARAMETER, not to the proc

`let s = b.build` is a PARENLESS UFCS CALL — `b.build` invokes `build(b)`, written with no parentheses and no call node, so it is invisible to a callee test. The analyzer used to publish nothing here at all; the differential oracle shared the omission, so the lane reported 0% unexplained on a shape both got wrong

forbidRelationships.comment: Nim's `echo` is a compiler builtin, never a call target (NIM_BUILTINS)
a numeric conversion is a builtin, not a user call

`Rect(name: "r", w: w, …)` NAMES the field `name`; it does not read it. Nim has no ternary, so `x: value` in an expression only ever names a field of a construction or a variant branch. Constrained by SOURCE because a legitimate read of the same field exists — `method describe(s: Shape) = s.name` — and a target-only pin would forbid both

`let (_, fileStem, _) = splitFile(path)` binds `fileStem` LOCALLY, so the read below it is a read of the local, not of `FileInfo.fileStem`. The pre-fix frame binder took only children typed symbol_declaration and skipped the wrapping tuple_deconstruct_declaration whole, so the binding was never in scope and this read was attributed to the struct property declared 60 lines earlier. Not a dangling edge — the target is a real symbol — so no dangling check could ever have caught it
`written = b.parts.len` is a WRITE. The right-hand side is the read; the left side is the target. Constrained by source because the read of `written` elsewhere in the file is legitimate

the callee of a call is a `calls` edge and NOT also a `uses` read — one call site, one edge. The pre-fix read pass did not exclude the callee subtree, so every call site produced two edges to one target

the `x` of `type Addable = concept x` is a concept's formal PARAMETER and the reads in its body `(x + x) is SomeNumber` are reads of that binding, not of any value. A concept is the one formal parameter in Nim written with no symbol_declaration wrapper and no type annotation, so nothing else in the read pass recognised it

note: This fixture's value is the FORBID half as much as the expect half: it pins that locals/params/keywords/builtins stay OUT of the symbol and call graphs, which is the class of phantom every M12 defect has been.

expectComplexity.comment: a decision count over the analyzer's own grammar-derived cyclomatic rule: the `for`, the `try`, and the `except` branch are the three decision points
the `for` range is one decision point, so a bare loop is 2 and not 1 — a complexity measure that scored every file 1 would pass this suite vacuously
a straight-line body is 1, which is what makes the two rows above discriminating

expectImports.comment: `import std/[os, strutils]` is a module LIST; the element carries the list marker and the path is `prefix/element`

a THREE-segment path — the shape the pre-fix path reader dropped wholesale, because the grammar types the separator as a named `operator` node whose text is the whole token, so `op.type` is never `/`. 171 such imports across 141 corpus files published no edge at all
a single-segment relative import keeps the written spelling
a parent-relative import is a path, not dropped for lacking a `/` segment

the `from … import` form over a RELATIVE module. The pre-fix code had a second path reader here that recursed to identifier leaves, so this published `./mac`'s module as `mac` while the sibling `import ./configure` published `./configure`: two spellings for one module in one graph

expectDecorators.comment: `{.inline.}` is a calling-convention contract on a proc
`{.base.}` marks the ROOT of the override chain — without it the overrides edge is unexplainable from the symbol alone, since two methods share the name `describe`
